title: THEY TOLD YOU THAT IF YOU DON'T SPEAK IN TONGUES, YOU DON'T HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT. BUT IS THAT WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY SAID?
paragraphs: THEY TOLD YOU THAT IF YOU DON'T SPEAK IN TONGUES, YOU DON'T HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT. BUT IS THAT WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY SAID?
The painful question dividing Christians, the misunderstood miracle of Pentecost, and the biblical truth that could finally set a wounded believer free.
Imagine standing in a church filled with people worshiping God.
Hands are raised. Tears are falling. Voices are rising in languages you cannot understand.
Someone beside you begins speaking in tongues. Another person falls to their knees, overwhelmed with emotion. The preacher declares that the Holy Spirit is moving.
And you believe Him.
You love Jesus. You believe He died for your sins. You have confessed Him as Lord. You have cried out to Him in the darkest moments of your life. You have repented of things nobody else knows about.
But then someone places a hand on your shoulder and asks a question that quietly tears through your confidence.
"Have you received the Holy Spirit? Have you spoken in tongues yet?"
You hesitate.
"No."
Their expression changes.
"Then you need to keep praying until you receive Him."
And suddenly, something happens inside you that nobody in the room can see.
You begin questioning everything.
Was my salvation real?
Did God reject me?
Why can everyone else experience something I cannot?
Is there something wrong with my faith?
You return home that evening, carrying a burden you never expected to bring out of a worship service.
And perhaps the most painful thought comes when you finally lie down to sleep.
"Jesus, if You really live inside me, why can't I do what they do?"
If you have ever asked that question, please stay with me.
Because the answer is not found in the loudest voice in the sanctuary.
It is found in the Word of God.
And the truth may challenge both those who insist every Christian must speak in tongues and those who dismiss the gift altogether.
This is not an attack against Pentecostal Christians, charismatic believers, or anyone who sincerely practices spiritual gifts.
Nor is it an attempt to explain away the supernatural power of the Holy Spirit.
This is about something infinitely more important.
We must never require as proof of belonging to Jesus what Scripture does not require of every believer.
And we must never reject what God has genuinely given simply because we have seen people misuse it.
The Bible gives us a much more beautiful, challenging, and Christ-centered picture.
Let's begin in Jerusalem.
Not in a modern worship service.
Not in a theological debate.
But in an upstairs room where frightened disciples were waiting for a promise that would change the world.
Jesus had been crucified.
The One they followed had been publicly humiliated, nailed to a cross, and buried in a borrowed tomb.
But death had not held Him.
The risen Christ appeared to His followers, restored their hope, and commanded them to wait for the promised Holy Spirit.
In Acts 1:8, Jesus declared:
"But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me..." (KJV)
Notice what Jesus emphasized.
Power to be His witnesses.
Not spiritual superiority.
Not an opportunity to divide believers into first-class and second-class Christians.
Not a performance to prove who was closer to heaven.
The promised power was for the mission of Christ.
Then came Pentecost.
Acts 2 describes a sound like a mighty rushing wind, tongues appearing like fire, and believers being filled with the Holy Spirit.
They began speaking in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.
The Greek expression in Acts 2:4 is:
ἑτέραις γλώσσαις — heterais glōssais
It means "other tongues" or "different languages."
The word glōssa can refer to the physical tongue or to a language, depending on context.
And the context of Acts 2 is extraordinary.
People from different nations heard the disciples declaring the wonderful works of God in their own languages.
The crowd was astonished.
These were Galileans.
How were they speaking languages they had not learned?
It was a miracle.
Not a manufactured religious experience.
Not something the disciples rehearsed.
Not a technique taught by an enthusiastic leader.
The Holy Spirit empowered ordinary people to proclaim God's mighty works across linguistic boundaries.
And Peter explained that this event fulfilled the promise associated with Joel's prophecy: God would pour out His Spirit, and His people would prophesy.
Young and old.
Men and women.
Servants and free.
The message was astonishing.
God was pouring out His Spirit in fulfillment of His redemptive promise.
And the exalted Jesus was the One pouring Him out.
But here is where we must ask a question that many believers are afraid to ask.
Does the fact that believers spoke in tongues at Pentecost mean that every Christian in every generation must speak in tongues to prove they have received the Holy Spirit?
We cannot answer that question with emotion alone.
We must examine the whole counsel of Scripture.
Because Acts records several remarkable occasions when people received the Holy Spirit.
And those occasions are not all described identically.
In Acts 10, Peter preached the Gospel to Cornelius and his household.
These were Gentiles.
People whom many Jewish believers would not have expected to receive the same covenant blessing in the same way.
While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon those who heard the message.
The Jewish believers accompanying Peter were astonished.
Why?
Because the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even upon the Gentiles.
And they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God.
This was significant.
God was demonstrating that Gentile believers were not outsiders to the Gospel.
They were being welcomed through Jesus Christ.
The miracle confirmed their inclusion.
In Acts 19, Paul encountered certain disciples in Ephesus who knew John's baptism but needed to hear more fully about Jesus.
After they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus and Paul laid hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them.
They spoke in tongues and prophesied.
Again, a remarkable manifestation.
Again, a real work of God.
Again, something we must not dismiss.
But there is another account that deserves our attention.
Acts 8 describes the Samaritans receiving the Holy Spirit through the ministry of Peter and John.
Simon the magician observed that something happened when the apostles laid hands on people.
But the text does not explicitly identify speaking in tongues as that manifestation.
Some Christians infer that tongues occurred.
Others caution that Scripture does not tell us.
The honest response is simple.
We must not turn an inference into an explicit biblical statement.
And there are other conversion accounts in Acts where speaking in tongues is not reported at all.
That does not prove it never occurred.
But it does mean the narrative does not consistently present tongues as a recorded requirement for every individual conversion.
Now consider the Apostle Paul.
This is where the question becomes impossible to avoid.
Paul was not hostile to speaking in tongues.
Quite the opposite.
In 1 Corinthians 14:18, he wrote:
"I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all." (KJV)
Paul valued the gift.
He practiced it.
He did not treat genuine spiritual manifestations as something embarrassing or spiritually inferior.
And in 1 Corinthians 14:39, he explicitly instructed believers not to forbid speaking in tongues.
But the same apostle wrote something that should stop every Christian from making tongues a universal test of salvation.
In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul described the Church as one body with many members.
Different gifts.
Different functions.
One Spirit.
Then he asked a series of rhetorical questions.
"Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles? Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?" (1 Corinthians 12:29–30, KJV)
Look closely at the Greek question concerning tongues:
μὴ πάντες γλώσσαις λαλοῦσιν;
Mē pantes glōssais lalousin?
Literally, "Do all speak in tongues?"
The Greek particle μή (mē) introduces a question that expects a negative answer.
In the flow of Paul's argument, the answer is no.
Not everyone has the same gift.
Not everyone has the same function.
Not everyone speaks in tongues.

Now, to represent the theological discussion fairly, some Pentecostal Christians distinguish between tongues as an initial sign accompanying baptism in the Holy Spirit and tongues as an ongoing congregational gift.
They argue that Paul's questions in 1 Corinthians 12 concern the distribution of ministry gifts, not necessarily the initial experience described in Acts.
That distinction deserves to be understood rather than caricatured.
However, Scripture does not explicitly establish that distinction as a universal rule requiring every Spirit-baptized Christian to speak in tongues.
And Paul's teaching gives us strong reason to be cautious about making one particular gift the defining evidence of the Spirit's presence in every believer.
Especially when we read what he says elsewhere.
Romans 8:9 contains a statement that every Christian needs to understand.
"Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." (KJV)
Paul identifies the Spirit's presence as essential to belonging to Christ.
But he does not say that every person who belongs to Christ must demonstrate that reality through tongues.
In Ephesians 1:13, Paul teaches that believers, having heard the Gospel and believed in Christ, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
And 1 Corinthians 12:13 declares:
"For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body..." (KJV)
The language is about the Spirit's work in uniting believers to Christ and His body.
Christians differ on how Spirit baptism, conversion, and subsequent experiences of empowerment should be understood in relation to one another.
Those differences should be discussed carefully.
But the New Testament does not authorize us to tell a person who truly trusts in Jesus Christ that they necessarily lack the Holy Spirit simply because they have never spoken in tongues.
And if you have been living under that accusation, please hear this.
Your inability to produce a particular spiritual manifestation is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
You may have been measuring your relationship with God by the wrong standard.
But we need to go even deeper.
Because there is another danger.
It is possible to become so obsessed with the manifestation of spiritual power that we lose sight of the purpose of spiritual power.
Think about the Corinthian church.
They were spiritually gifted.
They had tongues.
They had prophecy.
They had knowledge.
They had extraordinary experiences.
Yet Paul had to confront their divisions, pride, immaturity, sexual sin, and disorder.
Imagine that.
A church could be rich in spiritual manifestations and still desperately need spiritual correction.
And right between Paul's discussion of spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 and his instructions for worship in chapter 14, he placed one of the most penetrating chapters in the entire Bible.
First Corinthians 13.
"Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." (1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV)
The word translated "charity" in the King James Version is:
ἀγάπη — agapē
Love.
Not merely affection.
Not religious excitement.
But the kind of love that reflects God's character and seeks the good of others.
Paul's point is devastating.
A person may possess extraordinary gifts and still fail in the very thing that gives Christian service its proper character.
Without love, even the most impressive spiritual expression becomes empty noise.
Now picture two people sitting in the same church.
One speaks in tongues frequently but humiliates others, refuses correction, spreads gossip, and treats struggling Christians with contempt.
The other has never spoken in tongues but quietly cares for a sick parent, confesses sin, forgives an enemy, serves the poor, and keeps trusting Jesus through suffering.
Which person is demonstrating the character of Christ?
We cannot judge their entire spiritual condition from a brief description.
God knows the heart.
But Scripture makes one thing unmistakable.
Spiritual gifts must never become an excuse to neglect spiritual fruit.
Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit:
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Gentleness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Meekness.
Self-control.
These are not merely personality traits.
They are characteristics the Spirit cultivates in believers as they walk with Him.
And the most striking evidence of His transforming work may not be what happens during an emotionally charged worship service.
It may be what happens when nobody is watching.
When you could retaliate, but you choose forgiveness.
When temptation knocks, and you turn to Christ.
When pride rises, and you humble yourself.
When you fall into sin, and instead of hiding behind religious appearances, you confess and return to God.
When you are wounded, but you refuse to stop loving.
Not because these works earn salvation.
They do not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But because the grace that saves us also begins to transform us.
And that transformation matters.
Now perhaps someone reading this is thinking:
"But I speak in tongues, and I know God genuinely touched my life."
I am not here to tell you that your experience was false.
Scripture does not command Christians to reject every supernatural gift.
In fact, Paul wrote:
"Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues." (1 Corinthians 14:39, KJV)
If God has genuinely given you this gift, receive it with gratitude and humility.
Use it according to Scripture.
Do not be ashamed of it.
But please, do not turn your gift into a weapon against another believer.
Do not make someone feel spiritually worthless because their experience differs from yours.
And do not forget that every gift is given for God's glory, not our superiority.
Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 14 is particularly important.
He teaches that when tongues are exercised publicly in the gathered church, their use must be orderly and directed toward the building up of the congregation.
Where a tongue is addressed to the congregation, interpretation is necessary for the church to understand and benefit.

In 1 Corinthians 14:27–28, Paul limits public tongue-speaking to two or at most three speakers, each in turn, with interpretation. Without an interpreter, the speaker is to remain silent in the church and speak to himself and to God.
That instruction is not a rejection of tongues.
It is a safeguard against confusion.
Paul also acknowledges prayer in tongues and distinguishes between speaking with the spirit and speaking with understanding (1 Corinthians 14:14–15).
Christians interpret some details of these passages differently, including the relationship between private prayer and public ministry.
But the governing principles are clear.
Love.
Edification.
Understanding.
Order.
And the glory of God.
"For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace..." (1 Corinthians 14:33, KJV)

If a spiritual practice becomes a way of intimidating people, manufacturing emotional pressure, or ranking Christians according to visible experiences, we have reason to examine whether that practice is being conducted according to the apostolic instructions.
And here is something else we must face.
Some believers have been pressured to imitate sounds they did not genuinely receive.
Some have been told to repeat syllables until something happens.
Some have feared disappointing their pastors or appearing spiritually deficient.
Others have encountered genuine spiritual experiences but were never taught how to evaluate them biblically.
The answer is not to mock those people.
The answer is to bring everything back under the authority of Scripture.
First Thessalonians 5:19–21 tells believers not to quench the Spirit, not to despise prophecies, but to test everything and hold fast to what is good.
That is a remarkable balance.
Do not extinguish genuine spiritual activity.
But do not accept every claim without discernment.
The Holy Spirit never needs deception to prove that He is real.
And no Christian should feel compelled to manufacture a spiritual gift to earn acceptance.
Now I want to speak directly to the person who has been silently carrying shame.
Maybe you have attended prayer meetings where everyone around you seemed to receive something you did not.
Maybe you have watched people weep, tremble, and speak in tongues while you stood there wondering why heaven felt silent.
Maybe you have questioned your salvation for years.
You love Christ.
You believe the Gospel.
You want to obey Him.
You are fighting sins that once controlled you.
You are learning to forgive.
You are growing in prayer.
But a voice keeps whispering:
"You're not a real Spirit-filled Christian."
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not begin with your ability to demonstrate a gift.
It begins with what Jesus Christ accomplished on the cross.
Jesus did not die so that Christians could compete over spiritual experiences.
He died to redeem sinners.
He rose again so that those who trust in Him could receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
And He gives the Holy Spirit to His people.
In John 14:16–17, Jesus promised another Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who would dwell with His disciples.
The Greek word translated "Comforter" is:
παράκλητος — paraklētos
A term often rendered Helper, Advocate, or Comforter, describing one called alongside to help.
What a beautiful promise.
The Spirit is not presented merely as a force that produces impressive moments.
He is the divine Helper who dwells with God's people.
He glorifies Christ (John 16:14).
He convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8).
He helps believers in their weakness (Romans 8:26).
He bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16).
He transforms believers increasingly into Christlikeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).
He empowers witness.
He distributes gifts according to His will (1 Corinthians 12:11).
And He leads us toward Jesus.
That is why we must be careful not to reduce His presence to one outward manifestation.
The Holy Spirit is not a spiritual trophy.
He is God.
And His work is much greater than any single gift.
But perhaps we also need to speak to those who have dismissed tongues entirely.
Some Christians have seen disorderly worship and concluded that every contemporary claim of tongues must be false.
Others hold a cessationist understanding, believing that certain miraculous gifts served a foundational role in the apostolic era and are no longer ordinarily given today.
Still others believe all the gifts described in the New Testament remain available as the Spirit wills.
Faithful Christians disagree on these questions.
Those disagreements should be examined through careful biblical interpretation rather than ridicule or fear.
Scripture commands us to test claims.
It also commands us not to despise what is genuinely from God.
And whatever our position, we should be able to agree on this:
No spiritual experience should become more important to us than the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.
Now consider a scene from Luke 10.
Jesus had sent out seventy disciples, and they returned rejoicing because even demons were subject to them through His name.
They were excited.
They had witnessed spiritual authority.
They had experienced remarkable things.
But Jesus redirected their joy.
"Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." (Luke 10:20, KJV)
Do you see it?
Jesus did not deny that something extraordinary had happened.
He redirected their attention toward a deeper reason for rejoicing.
Their belonging to God.
That should humble every one of us.
Whether we speak in tongues or do not.
Whether we have experienced miraculous healing or have spent years praying through sickness.
Whether our worship is outwardly expressive or quietly reverent.
Our deepest confidence must never rest in our spiritual achievements or experiences.
It must rest in Christ.
And here is the question that matters far more than whether you can speak in a language you never learned.
Have you truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ?
Have you acknowledged your sin?
Have you trusted in His death and resurrection?
Are you turning away from sin and learning to follow Him?
Do you love His Word?
Are you willing to be corrected by Scripture, even when it challenges your traditions?
Are you seeking to love God and your neighbor?
These questions do not invite us to earn God's acceptance through flawless behavior.
They invite us to examine whether our profession of faith is sincere and whether our lives are being shaped by the One we claim to follow.
Because a person can speak in tongues and still need repentance.
And a person who has never spoken in tongues may genuinely belong to Jesus.
The decisive issue is not whether we have duplicated another person's experience.
It is whether we belong to Christ through faith.
There is a heartbreaking irony in the way Christians sometimes handle this subject.
We proclaim a Savior who welcomes repentant sinners by grace.
Then we sometimes create environments where wounded believers feel they must prove themselves worthy of belonging.
We preach the cross.
Then we measure people by outward manifestations.
We celebrate the Holy Spirit.
Then we grieve one another through pride, suspicion, and condemnation.
It should not be this way.
Jesus prayed for the unity of His people in John 17.
Not unity at the expense of truth.
But unity grounded in the truth and in our shared relationship with Him.
We can discuss spiritual gifts seriously without treating fellow believers as enemies.
We can disagree without humiliating one another.
We can seek the Spirit's power without abandoning biblical discernment.
And we can honor genuine spiritual gifts without making them a requirement that Scripture does not clearly impose upon every Christian.
Perhaps that is where some of us need to repent.
Not necessarily for believing that tongues are a gift.
Not necessarily for believing that tongues have ceased.
But for the arrogance with which we have treated people who disagree.
For confusing our interpretation with unquestionable authority.
For making wounded Christians feel unwelcome.
For allowing a debate about the Holy Spirit to produce behavior contrary to the fruit of the Holy Spirit.
Imagine if the next conversation about tongues sounded different.
Instead of asking someone, "Why haven't you spoken in tongues?"
We asked, "How can I help you grow closer to Jesus?"
Instead of saying, "You don't have the Spirit because you haven't had my experience,"
We said, "Let's open the Scriptures together and seek to understand what God has promised."
Instead of mocking a believer's spiritual experience,
We listened carefully and tested it with humility.
Instead of making the church a stage for religious performance,
We made it a place where truth and love meet.
A place where the broken can find restoration.
Where the proud are called to repentance.
Where the confused are taught patiently.
Where sinners encounter the grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the Church was never meant to be a competition over who appears most anointed.
It is the body of Christ.
And every member needs the others.
Now let me bring this back to the question that began our journey.
Should Christians speak in tongues as evidence of receiving the Holy Spirit?
The New Testament clearly teaches that speaking in tongues is a genuine spiritual gift and that tongues accompanied the Spirit's coming upon believers on significant occasions in Acts.
Christians should not automatically condemn or forbid the genuine exercise of this gift.
But the New Testament does not clearly teach that every Christian must speak in tongues to prove they have received the Holy Spirit.
Paul explicitly teaches that the Spirit distributes gifts according to His will, and his rhetorical question in 1 Corinthians 12:30 expects that not everyone speaks in tongues.
Scripture places our belonging to Christ in the context of faith in Him and the Spirit's saving work, not a universal requirement to demonstrate one particular gift.
And while the fruit of the Spirit is not a substitute for the Gospel or a way of earning salvation, a transformed life provides meaningful evidence of the Spirit's sanctifying work.
So seek the Holy Spirit.
Pray for His empowering.
Be open to whatever gifts He chooses to give according to His Word.
Do not despise genuine gifts.
Do not imitate what you have not received.
Do not judge another Christian's salvation by a manifestation that Scripture does not universally require.
And above all, do not allow the pursuit of spiritual experiences to replace your pursuit of Jesus.
Because the Spirit who descended at Pentecost is the same Spirit who glorifies the crucified and risen Christ.
He is not competing with Jesus for our attention.
He is leading us to Him.
And maybe this is the moment when you finally stop asking:
"Why am I not like that other Christian?"
And begin praying:
"Lord Jesus, make me more like You."
More faithful.
More humble.
More loving.
More obedient.
More willing to repent.
More courageous in witnessing.
More sensitive to the truth.
More surrendered to the Spirit's work.
That prayer may not attract a crowd.
It may not produce a dramatic video.
It may not impress the person standing beside you.
But a life increasingly conformed to Christ is never insignificant in the sight of God.
And if you have spent years feeling spiritually inferior because you have never spoken in tongues, I want you to remember something.
Jesus did not purchase your redemption with His blood only to leave your assurance dependent upon reproducing someone else's spiritual experience.
Look to Him.
Trust His Gospel.
Receive what His Word teaches.
And walk with Him in faith.
If this article exposed a hidden fear, healed a misunderstanding, or challenged something you have believed for years, I would love to hear your story.
Let's make the conversation a place of biblical truth, humility, and love, not another battlefield where Christians wound one another.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still seeking the truth about Jesus to follow along.
Because there are too many people who know the language of religion but have never truly understood the beauty of the Gospel.
And this is why Gospel Warrior continues to create and share Christ-centered teaching.
Behind every article is the desire to reach another person who is struggling, questioning, repenting, healing, or discovering Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not pressured or compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and faithful stewardship of whatever He has entrusted to you.
These resources are intended to help you move beyond a passing emotional moment into lasting biblical understanding, prayer, spiritual growth, and faithful discipleship.
And if you are not able to give financially, you can still help tremendously.
Invite someone to read it.
Pray for this ministry.
Encourage others to open their Bibles.
Help us carry the message of Jesus Christ beyond the walls of one church, one community, or one nation.
Because the goal has never been to build a following around a personality.
It is to point people to the Savior.
And before you leave, I want to offer one final prayer.
Lord Jesus, forgive us for every time we have made spiritual gifts more important than spiritual love.
Forgive us when we have judged others harshly, trusted religious appearances, or allowed pride to distort Your truth.
Heal those who have been wounded by spiritual manipulation.
Correct those who have misused Your Word.
Give humility to those who teach and discernment to those who listen.
Fill Your people with courage, holiness, compassion, and love.
Grant us a deeper understanding of Your Holy Spirit, not so that we may boast about our experiences, but so that we may glorify You with our lives.
Teach us to welcome every genuine gift You give, reject what is false, and never lose sight of the Gospel.
And for the believer who has been lying awake at night, wondering whether You have forgotten them, draw their eyes back to Your cross, Your resurrection, and Your faithful promises.
In Your holy name, Jesus.
Amen.
You may never speak in a language the crowd cannot understand, but never forget that the Savior understands every broken prayer you whisper in faith.
